data.q: Which concurrency pattern uses a channel to signal completion of a goroutine, allowing the main function to wait for it?
o: Worker Pool
Fan-out, Fan-in
Done Channel (Completion Signal)
Pipeline
data.e: A 'done' channel (often of type struct{} or bool) is a common pattern to signal that a goroutine has finished its work, allowing synchronization without a WaitGroup.

data.q: In the 'Fan-out, Fan-in' pattern, what does 'Fan-out' refer to?
o: Multiplexing multiple channels into a single channel
Distributing work from one channel to multiple worker goroutines
Closing a channel when all senders are done
Buffering a channel to prevent blocking
data.e: Fan-out involves starting multiple goroutines reading from the same input channel to parallelize work processing. Fan-in is the multiplexing of multiple result channels into one.

data.q: What is the primary purpose of the `sync.WaitGroup` in Go concurrency patterns?
o: To protect shared memory access (Mutual Exclusion)
To wait for a collection of goroutines to finish execution
To communicate data between goroutines via channels
To limit the number of concurrent goroutines
data.e: WaitGroup is used to block until a counter of active goroutines reaches zero. It is distinct from Mutex (protection) or Semaphore (limiting concurrency).

data.q: Which pattern is best suited for limiting the number of concurrent operations (e.g., limiting API calls to 10 at a time)?
o: Pipeline
Worker Pool (using a buffered channel as a semaphore)
Pub/Sub
Generator
data.e: A Worker Pool implemented with a buffered channel (semaphore) or a fixed number of workers consuming from a job queue effectively limits concurrency.

data.q: What characterizes a 'Pipeline' pattern in Go?
o: Multiple stages connected by channels, where each stage is a goroutine processing data and passing to the next
A single goroutine broadcasting messages to many subscribers
A mutex protecting a shared map
A function that returns a channel and spawns a goroutine to push data
data.e: Pipelines chain stages (functions reading from in-chan, writing to out-chan) allowing data to flow through transformation steps concurrently.

data.q: How does the 'Generator' pattern differ from a standard function returning a slice?
o: It returns a channel and produces values asynchronously in a goroutine
It blocks the caller until all values are computed
It uses a Mutex to protect the returned data
It panics if the channel buffer is full
data.e: Generators return a read-only channel (`<-chan T`) and spawn a goroutine to push data, enabling lazy evaluation and streaming, unlike slices which hold all data in memory at once.

data.q: What is the correct way to implement 'Fan-in' (multiplexing) safely?
o: Have multiple goroutines write to the same channel without synchronization
Use a single goroutine to read from multiple input channels using a `select` statement
Close all input channels immediately after starting workers
Use a Mutex to lock the output channel before writing
data.e: Fan-in is typically implemented by a dedicated goroutine that uses `select` to read from multiple input channels and write to a single output channel. Channels are thread-safe for multiple writers, but the fan-in logic usually centralizes reading.

data.q: In the 'Context' pattern for cancellation, what happens when `ctx.Done()` channel is closed?
o: The program exits immediately
All goroutines listening on that context should stop work and return
The garbage collector runs
A panic is triggered in the parent goroutine
data.e: Closing the `Done` channel is a broadcast signal. Goroutines should `select` on `ctx.Done()` and return/clean up when it fires, implementing cooperative cancellation.

data.q: Which pattern involves a goroutine that manages a specific piece of state (like a map or counter) and other goroutines communicate with it via channels to read/write that state?
o: Mutex Guard
Monitor Goroutine (or Actor Pattern)
Pipeline
Worker Pool
data.e: This is the Monitor Goroutine pattern (similar to Actor model). Instead of using Mutexes, ownership of the state is confined to a single goroutine; others send requests via channels.

data.q: What is the idiomatic Go way to handle a 'Producer-Consumer' scenario where the producer might be faster than the consumer?
o: Use an unbuffered channel to force synchronization (backpressure)
Use a buffered channel to absorb bursts
Use a Mutex and a slice
Spawn unlimited goroutines for consumers
data.e: Buffered channels decouple producer and consumer speeds up to the buffer capacity, handling bursts. Unbuffered channels enforce strict synchronization (blocking producer until consumer ready).

data.q: When using `errgroup.Group`, what happens if one goroutine returns an error?
o: The error is ignored, and all goroutines continue running
The group cancels the context (if configured), waits for others, and returns the first error
The program panics immediately
Only the failing goroutine stops; others run to completion silently
data.e: `errgroup` (with context) cancels the derived context on first error, signals other goroutines to stop (via context cancellation), waits for all, and returns the first non-nil error.

data.q: What is the primary risk of reading from a closed channel in a `for range` loop vs a manual `ok` check?
o: `for range` panics on closed channel, manual check does not
`for range` exits cleanly when channel is closed, manual check requires explicit `ok` verification to distinguish zero value from closure
Manual check is faster
There is no difference
data.e: `for range c` automatically terminates when `c` is closed. Manual `v, ok := <-c` requires checking `ok` to know if the channel closed (returning zero value) vs a valid zero value sent.

data.q: Which pattern is described by: 'Do not communicate by sharing memory; instead, share memory by communicating'?
o: Mutex/Lock Pattern
Channel/Message Passing Pattern (CSP)
Atomic Operations Pattern
Thread-Local Storage Pattern
data.e: This is the core Go proverb advocating for CSP (Communicating Sequential Processes) using channels over traditional shared-memory locking.

data.q: How do you implement a 'Rate Limiter' pattern using Go concurrency primitives?
o: Using a `time.Ticker` channel to gate operations in a loop or select statement
Using `time.Sleep` inside every goroutine
Using a global counter protected by a Mutex
Using an unbuffered channel for every request
data.e: A `time.Ticker` provides a channel that fires at intervals. Consuming from this channel (or a buffered 'token bucket' channel refilled by a ticker) effectively limits throughput.

data.q: What is the purpose of the 'Or-Done' channel helper pattern?
o: To merge two done channels into one that closes when either closes
To run two functions simultaneously
To prevent a channel from closing
To buffer a done channel
data.e: The `orDone` pattern (often a helper function) takes a parent `done` channel and a data channel. It returns a new channel that closes if *either* the parent context is done or the data channel closes, preventing goroutine leaks in pipelines.

data.q: In a 'Worker Pool' pattern, why is it important to close the `jobs` channel?
o: To prevent the workers from panic
To signal to the worker goroutines (range loops) that no more jobs will arrive, allowing them to exit gracefully
To free up the channel memory immediately
To increase the buffer size
data.e: Workers typically use `for job := range jobs`. Closing `jobs` terminates the range loop, allowing the worker goroutine to finish and `wg.Done()` to be called. Forgetting to close causes workers to hang forever.
